overview: I3206 closes the I32 block by connecting fuel accountability, approach-entry routing, and localizer sensing discipline. The event standard is to know when fuel burn has drifted from the plan, when a feeder segment authorizes descent, and how to prevent reverse-sensing traps.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: En route fuel management uses the planned Estimated Fuel Remaining for each leg as a benchmark against the Actual Fuel Remaining in the aircraft.

children.text: Verify the actual fuel load before flight; a normal T-6B single-point refuel planning load is 1100 pounds, but the gauges are the aircraft truth source.
Build EFR during planning by subtracting start, taxi, takeoff fuel and then each leg's planned fuel from the remaining fuel line above it.
At the end of each leg, compare AFR to EFR. AFR greater than or equal to EFR means the plan is still supported; AFR less than EFR requires immediate investigation.
Make the fuel comparison part of the OPS Check so it happens before the aircraft is already boxed into a low-fuel decision.
Common reasons for AFR shortfall are less fuel onboard at takeoff than planned, higher climb or cruise fuel flow, slower groundspeed, flight-log math error, or a fuel leak.
The earlier the cause is identified, the more useful the options are: adjust power or routing, request priority handling, divert, or transition to a fuel-conservation profile as appropriate.
If fuel endurance becomes the controlling factor, use NATOPS max-endurance guidance rather than guessing at a low-burn technique.
The DRAFT report organizes a divert request: Destination, Route, Altitude, Fuel remaining in hours plus minutes, and Time en route to the alternate.
The workbook builds that data from the flight log so the divert call can be read instead of improvised under pressure.
For DD Form 1801 endurance, use the planned profile: time from takeoff to destination fix plus fuel remaining at that fix converted to hours and minutes.

items.text: A feeder fix is the fix that begins a feeder route from en route structure toward an IAF or other approach-entry point.

children.text: Feeder fixes are often shown with thin arrows rather than the thick NoPT track used for a straight-in entry.
A feeder fix that is not labeled NoPT or IAF is not itself the approach entry; it is the start of the published route to the IAF.
Use the chart language and symbology to decide whether you are cleared onto a feeder route, direct to an IAF, or onto a NoPT transition.
If cleared for the approach while tracking inbound from a feeder fix, descend only to the higher of the feeder-route altitude or the IAF crossing altitude.
At the IAF, execute the published approach procedures for that entry instead of carrying feeder-route habits into the terminal segment.
The feeder fix solves route transition; it does not automatically cancel altitude assignments or authorize a procedure turn unless the approach clearance and chart support it.

items.text: Feeder routes connect en route structure to an IAF, IF, or other published approach segment and become part of the approach clearance when assigned or accepted.

children.text: Follow the published course and altitude along the feeder route to the IAF or IF.
If cleared direct or vectored to join an approach, maintain the last assigned ATC altitude until established on a published segment and cleared for the approach or cleared lower.
Once established on the published segment, descend no lower than the minimum altitude published for that segment.
At least one feeder route may exist, but multiple feeder routes or transitions can feed the same approach; choose the one that matches the clearance.
Do not treat a feeder route as an informal shortcut. It carries charted course, altitude, and entry consequences.
When the chart uses NoPT on a thick track, the no-procedure-turn entry is explicit; when that label is absent, confirm whether the route only feeds an IAF.

items.text: CDI reverse sensing is a localizer setup error: the needle appears to command the opposite correction when the CDI course is set to the wrong side of the localizer.

children.text: For normal ILS or LOC approaches, set the front course depicted for the final approach course.
For LOC BC approaches, identify and set the true front course, which is the reciprocal of the depicted back-course final approach course.
In the T-6B, selecting the correct front course prevents reverse sensing whether flying a back course or outbound on a front course.
If the back course itself is set into the CDI on a LOC BC, expect reverse sensing.
Tune, identify, and monitor the localizer as soon as practical during the transition, then set PFD source to LOC when ready for localizer tracking.
Course and glideslope indications are reliable only when warning flags or red Xs are absent, the localizer identifier is received, and the aircraft is within usable range.
Expect localizer sensitivity to increase near the transmitter; inside the FAF, use small heading corrections near the wind-corrected heading instead of chasing the needle.
For a LOC BC final, disregard glideslope indications and fly the non-precision profile to the published MDA and MAP.

If full-scale CDI deflection occurs between the FAF and MAP, turn to reestablish and track the localizer while climbing to the missed-approach altitude, unless a published maximum altitude restricts the climb before the MAP.

Common errors are setting the back course in the CDI, flying through final, overcorrecting, continuing with full-scale deflection inside the FAF, and executing the missed at MDA instead of at the MAP.

studyNotes.summary: Use EFR versus AFR to catch fuel drift early, read feeder fixes and routes as charted clearance structure, and set the correct front course before trusting localizer CDI sensing.

summary: Fuel checks, feeder-route approach entries, and localizer reverse-sensing prevention.
